items.signature: line y = mx + 30, point (8, 58) residual -6 -> predicted 64 -> m = 4.25; traps 2.75 (sign), 3.5 (residual ignored)
items.stem: The line of best fit for a data set is $y = mx + 30$, where $m$ is a constant. For the data point $(8, 58)$, the actual $y$-value minus the predicted $y$-value is $-6$. What is the value of $m$?

common_wrong.feedback: Uses predicted $= 52$, which reverses the residual sign.
Solves $8m + 30 = 58$, which ignores the residual.

solution.key_idea: The residual turns the data point into a point on the line: prediction $=$ actual $-$ residual. That point gives an equation for $m$.
solution.steps:
The question asks for the slope $m$.
$58 - \text{predicted} = -6$ (actual minus predicted)
predicted $= 64$ (so the line passes through $(8, 64)$)
$8m + 30 = 64$ (substitute $x = 8$)
$8m = 34$ (subtract 30)
$m = \frac{17}{4} = 4.25$ (divide by 8)
The point $(8, 58)$ itself is 6 below the line, which is why the line value at $x = 8$ is larger than 58.
solution.be_careful: Use the point on the line, $(8, 64)$, not the data point $(8, 58)$.

items.signature: y = 0.9x + 6 (test 1 -> test 2); A 20 higher on test 1; actual test 2: A 81, B 70 -> residual A minus residual B = 11 - 18 = -7; traps 7, -9
items.stem: For a class, the line of best fit $y = 0.9x + 6$ relates each student’s score $y$ on a second test to the score $x$ on a first test. Student A scored 20 points higher than student B on the first test. On the second test, student A scored 81 and student B scored 70. What is (student A’s actual score minus predicted score) minus (student B’s actual score minus predicted score) on the second test?

common_wrong.feedback: Computes $18 - 11$, the reverse order.
Uses a prediction gap of 20 instead of $0.9(20) = 18$.

solution.key_idea: The difference of two residuals is (difference of actual values) minus (difference of predictions). The predictions differ by slope times the gap in $x$, and the intercept cancels.
solution.steps:
The question asks for residual A minus residual B.
Let $b$ be student B’s first-test score, so student A’s is $b + 20$.
predicted A $-$ predicted B $= 0.9(b + 20) - 0.9b = 18$ (slope times the gap of 20)
actual A $-$ actual B $= 81 - 70 = 11$ (second-test scores)
(A residual) $-$ (B residual) $= 11 - 18 = -7$ (regroup actual minus predicted)
The first-test scores themselves are not needed.
solution.check: Try $b = 60$: predictions 60 and 78, residuals $70 - 60 = 10$ and $81 - 78 = 3$, and $3 - 10 = -7$ ✓
solution.be_careful: Neither first-test score is needed. The intercept 6 cancels.

items.signature: y = 3x + c, x = years since 2005; rewritten with t = years since 2012 the intercept is 2c -> 21 + c = 2c, c = 21; predict 2015 -> 51; traps 9 (shift reversed), 21 (stopped at c)
items.stem: A line of best fit for the attendance $y$, in hundreds of people, at a yearly festival is $y = 3x + c$, where $x$ is the number of years since 2005 and $c$ is a constant. When the same line is written in terms of $t$, the number of years since 2012, its $y$-intercept is $2c$. According to the line of best fit, what is the predicted attendance, in hundreds of people, for the year 2015?

common_wrong.feedback: Uses $x = t - 7$, which gives $c = -21$ and then $30 - 21 = 9$.
This is $c$. The question asks for the prediction for 2015.

solution.key_idea: Writing the same line with a later starting year keeps the slope and replaces the intercept by the line’s value at the new start. That fact gives an equation for $c$.
solution.steps:
The question asks for the prediction for 2015. First find $c$.
Step 1: Relate the two inputs.
2012 is 7 years after 2005, so $x = t + 7$ (years since 2005 are 7 more)
Step 2: Rewrite the line.
$y = 3(t + 7) + c = 3t + 21 + c$ (substitute and distribute)
new $y$-intercept $= 21 + c$ (the value when $t = 0$, that is, in 2012)
Step 3: Use the given intercept.
$21 + c = 2c$ (the new intercept is $2c$)
$c = 21$ (subtract $c$ from both sides)
Step 4: Predict for 2015.
2015 is $x = 10$ (10 years after 2005)
$y = 3(10) + 21 = 51$ (substitute)
The predicted attendance is 51 hundred people.
solution.be_careful: A later starting year means smaller inputs: $x = t + 7$, not $t - 7$.

items.signature: model A y = 2x + 10, model B y = -x + 40; one data point has residual 3 under A and -6 under B -> x = 7, y = 27; traps 7 (x only), 24
items.stem: Two linear models are fitted to the same data. Model A is $y = 2x + 10$, and model B is $y = -x + 40$. For one data point, the actual $y$-value minus the value predicted by model A is 3, and the actual $y$-value minus the value predicted by model B is $-6$. What is the actual $y$-value of this data point?

common_wrong.feedback: This is the $x$-value of the point, not the $y$-value.
This is model A’s prediction at $x = 7$, not the actual value.

solution.key_idea: Each residual turns into an equation linking the point’s $x$ and $y$. Two models give two equations, so the point is fixed.
solution.steps:
The question asks for the actual $y$-value of the point. Let the point be $(x, y)$.
$y - (2x + 10) = 3$, so $y = 2x + 13$ (residual under model A)
$y - (-x + 40) = -6$, so $y = -x + 34$ (residual under model B)
$2x + 13 = -x + 34$ (both describe the same $y$)
$3x = 21$ (add $x$, subtract 13)
$x = 7$ (divide by 3)
$y = 2(7) + 13 = 27$ (substitute back)
The point is $(7, 27)$: 3 above line A and 6 below line B.
solution.be_careful: The question asks for $y$, not $x$. Also, a negative residual means the point is below that line.

items.signature: population 2,000 at year 0 and 3,200 at year 4; linear L and exponential E both fit; year 2: L 2,600 > E about 2,530; year 8: E 5,120 > L 4,400
items.stem: A town’s population was 2,000 in year 0 and 3,200 in year 4. A linear model $L$ and an exponential model $E$ each give exactly these two values. Which statement correctly compares the predictions of the two models for year 2 and year 8?

choices.text: $E$ predicts more in both year 2 and year 8.
choices.feedback: Exponential growth does not beat linear growth everywhere. Between the two shared years the curve stays below the line.

choices.text: $L$ predicts more in both year 2 and year 8.
choices.feedback: After year 4 the exponential model multiplies by 1.6 every 4 years and passes the line: 5,120 versus 4,400.

choices.text: The two models predict the same value in year 2, and $E$ predicts more in year 8.
choices.feedback: Fitting the same two years does not make the models agree in between: 2,600 versus about 2,530.

choices.text: $L$ predicts more in year 2, and $E$ predicts more in year 8.

solution.key_idea: A linear model adds the same amount each year. An exponential model through the same two points multiplies by the same factor, so it rises slowly at first and fast later: below the line between the points, above it after.
solution.steps:
The question asks which model predicts more in year 2 and in year 8.
Step 1: Linear model.
$\frac{3,200 - 2,000}{4} = 300$ per year (constant change)
$L(2) = 2,600$ and $L(8) = 2,000 + 300(8) = 4,400$ (evaluate)
Step 2: Exponential model.
$\frac{3,200}{2,000} = 1.6$ every 4 years (constant ratio)
$E(8) = 3,200(1.6) = 5,120$ (four more years, one more factor of 1.6)
$E(2) = 2,000\sqrt{1.6} \approx 2,530$ (half of the 4-year period)
Step 3: Compare.
year 2: $2,600 > 2,530$ ($L$ is greater)
year 8: $5,120 > 4,400$ ($E$ is greater)
solution.be_careful: "Exponential is always greater" is false between the two shared points.
solution.desmos: Graph $y = 2,000 + 300x$ and $y = 2,000(1.6)^{x/4}$ and compare at $x = 2$ and $x = 8$.

items.signature: shipping y = 0.05x + 3 (x grams, y dollars); in kilograms X and cents Y: Y = 5000X + 300 -> slope 5000; traps 50 (kg only), 5 (cents only)
items.stem: A line of best fit for the shipping cost $y$, in dollars, of a package with a weight of $x$ grams is $y = 0.05x + 3$. The same line is rewritten to give the shipping cost $Y$, in cents, of a package with a weight of $X$ kilograms. What is the slope of the rewritten line?

common_wrong.feedback: Converts grams to kilograms but leaves the cost in dollars.
Converts dollars to cents but leaves the weight in grams.

solution.key_idea: Change the units one variable at a time: write the old input in terms of the new one, substitute, then convert the output. Each conversion multiplies the slope.
solution.steps:
The question asks for the slope of $Y$ in terms of $X$.
Step 1: Convert the input.
$X$ kilograms $= 1,000X$ grams, so $x = 1,000X$ (1 kilogram is 1,000 grams)
$y = 0.05(1,000X) + 3 = 50X + 3$ (dollars per kilogram)
Step 2: Convert the output.
$Y = 100y$ (1 dollar is 100 cents)
$Y = 100(50X + 3) = 5,000X + 300$ (distribute 100)
The slope of the rewritten line is 5,000 cents per kilogram, which is the same rate as 5 cents per gram.
solution.be_careful: Both conversions make the slope larger here: more grams in a kilogram and more cents in a dollar.

items.signature: line y = 2x + 5, x = 1,3,5,7, residuals 1,-2,k,3, mean actual 14.5 -> mean predicted 13, residual total 6, k = 4; traps 1.5 (mean residual), -2
items.stem: A data set has four points with $x$-values 1, 3, 5, and 7. The line of best fit for the data is $y = 2x + 5$. For these points, the values of actual $y$ minus predicted $y$ are 1, $-2$, $k$, and 3, respectively. The mean of the four actual $y$-values is 14.5. What is the value of $k$?

common_wrong.feedback: This is the mean residual, $\frac{6}{4}$, not $k$.
This is the total of the four residuals, not the single residual $k$.

solution.key_idea: Each actual value is its prediction plus its residual. So the total of the actual values is the total of the predictions plus the total of the residuals.
solution.steps:
The question asks for the missing residual $k$.
Step 1: Total of the actual values.
$4(14.5) = 58$ (mean times count)
Step 2: Total of the predictions.
predictions: $7, 11, 15, 19$ ($2x + 5$ at $x = 1, 3, 5, 7$)
$7 + 11 + 15 + 19 = 52$ (add)
Step 3: Total of the residuals.
$58 - 52 = 6$ (actual total minus predicted total)
$1 + (-2) + k + 3 = 6$ (the four residuals)
$k + 2 = 6$, so $k = 4$ (solve)
The third point is $(5, 19)$, which is 4 above the line.
solution.check: Actual values $8, 9, 19, 22$ total 58, and $\frac{58}{4} = 14.5$ ✓
solution.be_careful: The mean residual is 1.5, but the question asks for one residual, $k$.

items.signature: y = 500(1.21)^t, t years -> 1.21 = 1.1^2 so 10% every 6 months; traps 10.5% (halved rate), 21% per 6 months, 42% per 2 years
items.stem: An exponential model of best fit for the number of users $y$ of an app $t$ years after launch is $y = 500(1.21)^{t}$. According to the model, which of the following describes how the number of users changes?

choices.text: It increases by 10.5% every 6 months.
choices.feedback: This halves 21%. Two increases of 10.5% would give $1.105^2 \approx 1.221$, not 1.21.

choices.text: It increases by 10% every 6 months.
It increases by 21% every 6 months.
choices.feedback: 21% is the increase for a whole year, not half a year.

choices.text: It increases by 42% every 2 years.
choices.feedback: Two years multiply by $1.21^2 \approx 1.464$, an increase of about 46%, not 42%.

solution.key_idea: A factor per year can be split into equal factors for shorter periods: two half-years must multiply to the yearly factor, so each half-year factor is $\sqrt{1.21}$.
solution.steps:
The question asks for a correct description of the growth.
yearly factor $= 1.21$ (from the model)
half-year factor $f$ with $f \cdot f = 1.21$ (two half-years make a year)
$f = \sqrt{1.21} = 1.1$ (positive square root)
$y = 500(1.1)^{2t}$ (the same model in half-years)
factor 1.1 means an increase of 10% (each 6 months)
So the number of users increases by 10% every 6 months. Growth rates in an exponential model are not split by dividing the percent.
solution.be_careful: Half of 21% is not the half-year rate, because each half-year grows from a larger base.

solution.key_idea: The trend inside groups and the trend for all data together can point in opposite directions when the groups sit in different places.

items.signature: line predicts 40 at x = 10 and 70 at x = 30; P(10, a), Q(30, b), residuals opposite, b - a = 24 -> residual of P = 3; traps -3, 6, -6
items.stem: A line of best fit predicts $y = 40$ when $x = 10$ and $y = 70$ when $x = 30$. The data points $P(10, a)$ and $Q(30, b)$ have residuals (actual $y$ minus predicted $y$) that are opposites of each other, and $b - a = 24$. What is the residual for point $P$?

choices.feedback: This takes the whole gap $24 - 30 = -6$ as the residual of $Q$, then flips it, without splitting it between the two points.
This is the residual for $Q$. Point $P$ is above the line, and $Q$ is below it.
This is the gap $30 - 24$, which must be shared equally by the two opposite residuals.

solution.key_idea: Actual $=$ predicted $+$ residual at each point. The difference of the actual values is the difference of the predictions plus the difference of the residuals.
solution.steps:
The question asks for the residual $r$ at $P$. Then the residual at $Q$ is $-r$.
$a = 40 + r$ (actual at $P$)
$b = 70 - r$ (actual at $Q$)
$b - a = (70 - r) - (40 + r) = 30 - 2r$ (subtract)
$30 - 2r = 24$ (given)
$-2r = -6$ (subtract 30)
$r = 3$ (divide by $-2$)
So $P$ is 3 above the line and $Q$ is 3 below it. The actual values are $a = 40 + 3 = 43$ and $b = 70 - 3 = 67$, and their gap of 24 is smaller than the predicted gap of 30.
solution.check: $67 - 43 = 24$, and the residuals are $43 - 40 = 3$ and $67 - 70 = -3$ ✓
solution.be_careful: The predictions rise by 30 but the actual values rise only 24, so the left point must be above the line.

items.signature: f(x) = a(b)^x, f(2) - f(0) = 30, f(4) - f(2) = 75 -> b^2 = 2.5, a = 20, f(6) = 312.5; traps 125 (f(4)), 200 (constant difference), 245 (constant second difference)
items.stem: An exponential model $f(x) = a(b)^{x}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants and $b > 1$, predicts the number of members of a club $x$ months after it started. The model predicts an increase of 30 members from month 0 to month 2 and an increase of 75 members from month 2 to month 4. How many members does the model predict for month 6?

choices.feedback: 125 is the prediction for month 4. The question asks for month 6.
This adds 75 again, as if the increases were constant. That is linear thinking.
This assumes the increases themselves grow by a constant 45. In an exponential model the increases grow by a constant factor.

solution.key_idea: In an exponential model, the increases over equal time periods also grow by the same factor as the values. So the ratio of two increases gives the factor for one period.
solution.steps:
The question asks for $f(6)$.
Step 1: Find the factor for 2 months.
$f(2) - f(0) = a(b^2 - 1) = 30$ (first increase)
$f(4) - f(2) = ab^2(b^2 - 1) = 75$ (second increase)
$b^2 = \frac{75}{30} = 2.5$ (divide the second by the first)
Step 2: Find $a$.
$a(2.5 - 1) = 30$, so $a = 20$ (substitute $b^2 = 2.5$)
Step 3: Predict month 6.
$f(4) = 20(2.5)^2 = 125$ (two 2-month periods)
$f(6) = 125(2.5) = 312.5$ (one more period)
Each 2-month increase is 2.5 times the previous one: 30, 75, then 187.5, and $125 + 187.5 = 312.5$.
solution.check: Values 20, 50, 125, 312.5: the increases are 30, 75, and 187.5, each 2.5 times the last ✓
solution.be_careful: The model can predict a non-whole number of members; the question asks for the model’s prediction.

items.signature: plant A: y = 1.5w + 20 (weeks), plant B: y = 0.5d + 8 (days); B exceeds A by 10 when 3.5w + 8 - 1.5w - 20 = 10 -> w = 11; traps 6 (equal), 77 (days), 1 (A exceeds B by 10)
items.stem: The height of plant A, in centimeters, is modeled by $y = 1.5w + 20$, where $w$ is the number of weeks since planting. The height of plant B, in centimeters, is modeled by $y = 0.5d + 8$, where $d$ is the number of days since planting. Both plants were planted on the same day. According to the models, how many weeks after planting will the height of plant B be 10 centimeters greater than the height of plant A?

choices.feedback: This solves (plant A) minus (plant B) $= 10$. In week 1, plant A is the taller one.
This is when the two heights are equal. Plant B needs 5 more weeks to lead by 10.
This is the answer in days. The question asks for weeks.

solution.key_idea: Put both models on the same input before comparing them. A week is 7 days, so plant B grows $0.5(7) = 3.5$ centimeters per week.
solution.steps:
The question asks for the number of weeks $w$ at which B is 10 centimeters taller than A.
Step 1: Write plant B in weeks.
$d = 7w$ (7 days in a week)
$y = 0.5(7w) + 8 = 3.5w + 8$ (plant B in terms of $w$)
Step 2: Set up the gap.
$(3.5w + 8) - (1.5w + 20) = 10$ (B minus A equals 10)
$2w - 12 = 10$ (combine like terms)
$2w = 22$ (add 12)
$w = 11$ (divide by 2)
Plant B starts 12 centimeters shorter and gains 2 centimeters per week, so it is level at week 6 and 10 ahead at week 11.
solution.be_careful: Convert first. Comparing 1.5 per week with 0.5 per day directly makes plant B look slower.
